## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with arrhythmia on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. The overall enrichment pattern is dominated by inflammatory and cytokine-mediated mechanisms. The most statistically significant signal is cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, p = 1.0480055801033972 × 10−34, 65 associated proteins), followed by viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, p = 4.277640489045937 × 10−16, 27 associated proteins), tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (Reactome:R-HSA-5669034, p = 1.299783594479869 × 10−11, 14 associated proteins), and neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p = 5.793716961483522 × 10−10, 48 associated proteins). Taken together, these very low p-values and relatively large associated protein counts suggest a robust enrichment signal centered on immune activation. This pattern is consistent with literature indicating that inflammatory cytokines, innate immune activation, and infection-related signaling may alter ion channel function, gap junction coupling, calcium handling, and atrial or ventricular structural remodeling, thereby increasing susceptibility to arrhythmia.  

This inflammatory profile also connects naturally to a second major theme in the enrichment results, namely extracellular matrix turnover and tissue remodeling. Strong enrichment of collagen metabolic process (Gene Ontology:0032963, p = 3.1440856737905816 × 10−7, 14 associated proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p = 5.378474612832188 × 10−15, 30 associated proteins), and lung fibrosis (WikiPathways:WP3624, p = 8.265656098006917 × 10−7, 15 associated proteins) suggests that fibrotic remodeling may represent an important shared mechanism. This interpretation is supported by cardiac literature showing that excess collagen deposition and extracellular matrix reorganization can disrupt electrical conduction, promote conduction heterogeneity, and facilitate re-entry, which are central mechanisms in many forms of arrhythmia. The enrichment of endopeptidase activity (Gene Ontology:0004175, p = 2.7954040457582796 × 10−11, 44 associated proteins) further supports the possibility of active proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular environment, which may contribute to myocardial fibrosis and inflammatory tissue injury.  

Beyond inflammation and matrix remodeling, the enrichment profile may also point to changes in membrane organization and intracellular transport. Additional pathways, including lipid localization (Gene Ontology:0010876, p = 3.415223569846427 × 10−5, 26 associated proteins), late endosome (Gene Ontology:0005770, p = 0.007816926593059137, 16 associated proteins), and ruffle membrane (Gene Ontology:0032587, p = 0.041994677647457415, 6 associated proteins), suggest altered membrane trafficking, lipid handling, and receptor turnover. These processes are relevant because membrane composition and intracellular trafficking can influence ion channel localization, receptor signaling, and cardiomyocyte stress responses, all of which have been implicated in arrhythmia biology. Although some enriched annotations, such as colon goblet cells (Human Protein Atlas:0130891, p = 3.96653314155423 × 10−6, 36 associated proteins; Human Protein Atlas:0130893, p = 6.70451993364627 × 10−5, 21 associated proteins), pleural mesothelioma (WikiPathways:WP5087, p = 5.1660111075016064 × 10−5, 38 associated proteins), and arthralgia (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002829, p = 0.020265199832114434, 20 associated proteins), are less directly related to cardiac biology, they may reflect shared inflammatory, extracellular matrix, and secretory programs rather than tissue-specific causation. Overall, the pathway profile supports a model in which arrhythmia is linked to a convergence of cytokine-driven inflammation, immune cell activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis, and altered membrane trafficking, with the very low p-values providing strong statistical support for these mechanisms.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall enrichment structure in view, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Arthralgia (HP:0002829) 

Arthralgia refers to joint pain and is a clinical symptom rather than a discrete molecular signaling pathway. In biomedical interpretation, it usually reflects one of several underlying biological contexts, including systemic inflammation, autoimmune activation, infection-associated immune responses, metabolic or electrolyte disturbance, or treatment-related toxicity. Because joint pain commonly accompanies disorders with broad inflammatory or immune involvement, it can function as a clinical marker of multisystem disease rather than an isolated musculoskeletal complaint. The publications provided show that arthralgia appears in several settings relevant to heart rhythm disorders: as an adverse effect of anticancer therapy with Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibition, as a symptom in autoimmune diseases such as primary Sjogren syndrome and sarcoidosis, as part of infectious syndromes such as dengue, Lyme disease, and Zika virus infection, and in association with metabolic derangements such as severe magnesium deficiency. Thus, the biological significance of arthralgia in the present context is that it may identify disease states or treatment exposures that also affect cardiac conduction tissue, atrial and ventricular myocardium, autonomic balance, blood pressure regulation, calcium handling, or inflammatory injury, all of which can promote arrhythmia.  

Building on this clinical framing, the relationship between arthralgia and arrhythmia appears to be predominantly indirect, yet still clinically meaningful, because arthralgia often co-occurs with systemic conditions that may create an arrhythmogenic substrate. In autoimmune disease, transient or inflammatory arthralgia may accompany disorders with direct cardiac involvement; for example, primary Sjogren syndrome presenting with dry mouth and arthralgia was associated with complex arrhythmias, atrioventricular node dysfunction, and intraventricular conduction impairment, with improvement after glucocorticoid treatment, supporting an inflammatory mechanism linking the systemic syndrome to electrical instability of the heart (PubMed:26171561). A similar pattern is seen in sarcoidosis, in which arthralgia can accompany granulomatous disease that may involve the myocardium and lead to ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, conduction disease, arrhythmias, and heart failure (PubMed:36174882, PubMed:27454307). Infectious illnesses also illustrate this connection: dengue commonly presents with fever, myalgia, and arthralgia, yet can be complicated by atrial fibrillation and other rhythm disturbances, possibly through myocarditis, inflammatory cytokine activation, and altered intracellular calcium handling (PubMed:26500943, PubMed:38205141). Lyme disease and Zika virus infection likewise include arthralgia among systemic manifestations while also being linked to atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular block, myocarditis, and broader arrhythmic complications (PubMed:39391111, PubMed:33220438). Arthralgia may additionally signal treatment exposure relevant to arrhythmia risk: in trials of Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, arthralgia was a common adverse event, whereas atrial fibrillation and hypertension were notable cardiac toxicities, particularly with ibrutinib-containing therapy, indicating that joint pain and arrhythmia can emerge within the same drug-toxicity profile even if one does not directly cause the other (PubMed:29856685, PubMed:36400069). Finally, the coexistence of arthralgia and atrial fibrillation in severe magnesium deficiency emphasizes that shared systemic disturbances can produce both musculoskeletal symptoms and electrical instability (PubMed:31776649). Collectively, these studies indicate that arthralgia should be interpreted in arrhythmia research and clinical practice as a sentinel symptom of inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, or pharmacological states that may secondarily disrupt cardiac electrophysiology.[PubMed:36400069](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36400069) [PubMed:29856685](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29856685) [PubMed:26171561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26171561) [PubMed:36174882](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36174882) [PubMed:26500943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26500943) [PubMed:31776649](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31776649) [PubMed:39391111](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39391111) [PubMed:33220438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33220438) [PubMed:27454307](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27454307) [PubMed:38205141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38205141) 

With this clinical context in mind, the enrichment analysis may be viewed as a complementary layer that connects the symptom-level signal of arthralgia to biological processes potentially relevant to cardiac electrical instability. There were 20 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the biological context represented by arthralgia, which in this setting should be interpreted not as a single molecular pathway but as a clinically informative enrichment signal linking joint pain with systemic inflammation, autoimmune activation, infection-related immune responses, metabolic disturbance, treatment toxicity, and cardiac electrophysiological vulnerability. This enrichment pattern is biologically relevant to arrhythmia because the underlying conditions associated with arthralgia can converge on several arrhythmia-promoting mechanisms, including inflammatory injury to atrial and ventricular myocardium, altered autonomic regulation, disturbed calcium and magnesium homeostasis, blood pressure instability, and conduction system involvement. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 20 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

To move from the network-level view to gene-level interpretation, the following section introduces several proteins that may be of particular interest in relation to arrhythmia, while keeping the discussion cautious and grounded in the functions provided. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, ELN is one of the most compelling candidates for a meaningful connection with arrhythmia because abnormalities in elastin biology can directly affect vascular mechanics, ventricular afterload, and myocardial structural remodeling. ELN is essential for the mechanical integrity and elasticity of the aorta and other large vessels, and its role in smooth muscle cell maturation and extracellular matrix organization suggests that its dysfunction could promote arterial stiffness, altered hemodynamics, and secondary cardiac remodeling. Such remodeling is a well-established substrate for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. In addition, ELN participates in collagen fibril assembly and elastin cross-linking via LOX-related pathways, linking it to broader fibrotic and matrix-remodeling processes that can disrupt electrical conduction indirectly through myocardial fibrosis. Its reported involvement in angiotensin-related vascular smooth muscle regulation is also notable, because renin-angiotensin signaling is strongly implicated in atrial fibrosis and arrhythmogenesis. Therefore, although ELN is not a classical ion-channel gene, it stands out as a plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility through vascular dysfunction, extracellular matrix remodeling, and electromechanical coupling abnormalities.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

Continuing from extracellular elastic structure to broader matrix organization, COL5A1 is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its role in extracellular matrix architecture. Although type V collagen is a relatively minor fibrillar collagen, it is important in connective tissue organization and likely influences collagen fibrillogenesis and tissue mechanical properties. In the heart, perturbation of collagen composition can alter myocardial stiffness, chamber compliance, and conduction properties by promoting interstitial fibrosis or abnormal matrix organization. These changes are central to the development of arrhythmogenic substrates, particularly in atrial fibrillation and scar-related ventricular arrhythmias. The ability of COL5A1 to interact with matrix-associated molecules such as thrombospondin and glycosaminoglycans further supports a role in broader matrix signaling networks. Thus, COL5A1 stands out as a structurally relevant gene whose dysregulation could contribute indirectly to arrhythmia by modifying myocardial extracellular matrix composition and favoring conduction heterogeneity.  

Shifting from extracellular structure to nuclear organization, LMNB2 is noteworthy because defects in nuclear envelope biology are increasingly recognized in cardiomyopathy syndromes that carry substantial arrhythmic risk. The nuclear lamina is critical for maintaining nuclear structural integrity and regulating chromatin organization, and disruption of these processes can alter gene expression programs essential for cardiomyocyte survival, mechanical resilience, and electrical stability. While LMNA is the prototypical lamin gene associated with conduction disease and malignant ventricular arrhythmias, the functions described for LMNB2 place it in a related biological framework. Disturbance of nuclear architecture may predispose to myocardial dysfunction, cellular stress responses, and maladaptive remodeling, all of which can create an arrhythmogenic substrate. Therefore, LMNB2 should be considered a potentially relevant structural-regulatory factor, especially in the context of inherited cardiomyopathy or conduction system disease.[PubMed:28241138](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28241138)  

From structural remodeling, the discussion next extends to cardiometabolic mechanisms. PCSK9 is highly relevant to arrhythmia from a cardiometabolic perspective. Its central role in low-density lipoprotein receptor degradation and cholesterol homeostasis links it strongly to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, ischemic myocardial injury, and subsequent scar formation, all of which are major substrates for ventricular arrhythmias. Beyond this indirect but clinically important connection, PCSK9 also influences receptor trafficking and proteostatic pathways, suggesting broader effects on cellular stress responses. The reported reduction of epithelial sodium channel surface expression is not a canonical cardiac arrhythmia mechanism, but it underscores that PCSK9 can modulate membrane protein abundance. In practice, the strongest arrhythmia-related relevance of PCSK9 is likely through promotion of coronary artery disease and ischemic remodeling, which increase the risk of atrial and ventricular rhythm disorders. Thus, PCSK9 stands out not as a direct electrophysiological determinant, but as an important upstream driver of structural heart disease that can culminate in arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

A related but more inflammation-centered mechanism is suggested by PRTN3. PRTN3 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it links inflammation, vascular injury, and extracellular matrix degradation. Its proteolytic activity against elastin, laminin, fibronectin, and multiple collagens indicates a capacity to remodel tissue architecture extensively. In the cardiovascular system, excessive matrix degradation and inflammatory activation can contribute to endothelial dysfunction, myocardial injury, and fibrotic repair, all of which favor conduction abnormalities. The ability of PRTN3 to trigger inflammatory processes in neutrophils and participate in transendothelial migration further strengthens a plausible role in inflammatory arrhythmogenesis, particularly in settings such as myocarditis, vascular inflammation, or post-ischemic remodeling. Since inflammation is a recognized contributor to atrial fibrillation and other rhythm disorders, PRTN3 stands out as a biologically credible mediator of arrhythmia risk through immune-proteolytic pathways rather than direct ion-channel effects.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Because systemic mineral regulation is another recurring theme in arrhythmia biology, PTH1R may also warrant attention. PTH1R is particularly relevant to arrhythmia because calcium homeostasis is fundamental to cardiac excitability, action potential dynamics, and excitation-contraction coupling. Through its role in systemic calcium regulation, altered PTH1R signaling could contribute to hypercalcemia or broader calcium imbalance, both of which are known to affect cardiac conduction and repolarization. Clinically, disturbances in calcium metabolism can precipitate atrial and ventricular arrhythmias by modifying threshold potentials, triggered activity, and refractoriness. Although the function provided is centered on bone and renal calcium handling rather than direct cardiac signaling, the mechanistic link to arrhythmia is strong because systemic calcium perturbation is itself arrhythmogenic. Therefore, PTH1R deserves attention as an indirect but physiologically important determinant of rhythm stability.  

Extending from calcium balance to immune-remodeling interactions, SPP1 is a notable candidate because it connects immune activation with tissue remodeling, a combination highly relevant to arrhythmia. The described cytokine profile indicates a pro-inflammatory immune phenotype, favoring type I immune responses. In the heart, chronic inflammation promotes fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and electrical heterogeneity, particularly in atrial tissue. SPP1, also widely known as osteopontin, has been implicated in fibrotic and inflammatory remodeling in multiple cardiovascular contexts, making its inclusion particularly interesting. Even based solely on the listed function, its capacity to skew cytokine production toward a pro-inflammatory state supports a plausible role in atrial fibrillation, post-injury remodeling, and myocarditis-associated arrhythmias. Thus, SPP1 stands out as a likely mediator of inflammation-driven arrhythmogenic remodeling.  

A mechanistically related line of reasoning applies to TNFRSF11B. TNFRSF11B is of interest for arrhythmia because the function described prominently features intracellular calcium oscillations and reactive oxygen species generation, two processes that are central to cardiac arrhythmogenesis. Although the annotated context is osteoclast differentiation, the signaling logic is highly relevant: prolonged calcium oscillations and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species are known to promote triggered activity, cellular stress, and remodeling in cardiomyocytes. In addition, its immunoregulatory functions suggest a potential role in inflammatory disease states that can secondarily affect the myocardium. Therefore, TNFRSF11B may not be a direct arrhythmia gene in the classical sense, but it stands out mechanistically because it operates in pathways—calcium signaling, reactive oxygen species production, and immune regulation—that are deeply implicated in rhythm disorders.[PubMed:22664871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664871)  

In a similar tentative framework, TNFRSF13B may be relevant through protein handling and calcium-linked signaling. TNFRSF13B is potentially relevant to arrhythmia through two main mechanisms. First, its role in tail-anchored protein delivery to the endoplasmic reticulum suggests it contributes to membrane protein biogenesis and trafficking, processes that are highly important for ion channels and other proteins governing cardiac excitability. Disruption of protein targeting or membrane insertion can alter cellular electrophysiology indirectly. Second, its involvement in intracellular calcium elevation, although described in T cells, points to broader biology connected to calcium signaling, a core determinant of arrhythmia. Its role in B-cell survival also raises the possibility of immune-mediated effects on cardiac tissue in inflammatory settings. Overall, TNFRSF13B is not the strongest arrhythmia candidate on the list, but it is mechanistically interesting because it intersects protein trafficking, calcium signaling, and immunity.[PubMed:23041287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23041287) [PubMed:24392163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24392163) [PubMed:27226539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27226539) [PubMed:32187542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32187542) [PubMed:7522304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7522304)  

The immune-remodeling theme becomes even more apparent when considering TREM2. TREM2 stands out because it is deeply involved in innate immune activation and phagocytic responses, processes increasingly recognized as important in arrhythmia-associated cardiac remodeling. The broad immune signaling functions described here suggest that TREM2 can shape inflammatory tone, cytokine production, cell survival, and tissue remodeling. In the setting of cardiac injury, myocarditis, or chronic heart failure, dysregulated myeloid activation and macrophage behavior can promote fibrosis, alter gap-junction organization, and destabilize electrical conduction. TREM2-related pathways may therefore influence arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly through inflammatory remodeling rather than direct electrophysiological effects. Its role in multinucleated giant cell formation and osteoclast biology also reinforces its involvement in fusion and cytoskeletal programs that may mirror broader tissue-remodeling functions. Overall, TREM2 is a strong immunobiological candidate for contributing to arrhythmogenic substrates in inflammatory or remodeling-prone cardiovascular disease.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392)  

Finally, complementing the structural, inflammatory, and metabolic candidates above, ADA2 introduces a neurohumoral dimension that may also be relevant to rhythm regulation. ADA2 is directly relevant to arrhythmia because adrenergic signaling is a major regulator of heart rate, conduction, and triggered electrical activity. Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors modulate cyclic adenosine monophosphate generation through G-protein-mediated inhibition of adenylate cyclase, thereby influencing autonomic balance. Since sympathetic and parasympathetic tone strongly affect arrhythmia initiation and maintenance, especially in atrial fibrillation and stress-triggered ventricular arrhythmias, altered ADA2-related signaling could plausibly modify arrhythmia susceptibility. Although this receptor is not as classically implicated as beta-adrenergic pathways in cardiac electrophysiology, catecholamine signaling broadly is central to arrhythmic risk. Therefore, ADA2 is a noteworthy candidate because it connects neurohumoral regulation to electrophysiological instability.
